([`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named)), so a package can compute over a `tainted` value and return
it still `tainted`.

**Declined:**
- **Ambient capabilities: the process is granted, and every package inherits.** That is what every
  mainstream package system does, and it is how a compromised transitive dependency becomes a breach.
  No incumbent can retrofit the refusal.
- **A package inherits the application's defaults.** It would hand every dependency the files, hosts
  and programs a first program needs, which is the ambient authority above under another name.

**Not on disk.** `nvs pkg fetch` writes the grant lines (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/fetch.rs`), and
the compiler checks each call against them (`crates/nvs-types/src/capability.rs`). `nvs pkg add`,
which prints what a new dependency's subgraph requests, is not written yet.

<sub>See also [`security/authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace`](security.md#security-authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace), [`security/grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace`](security.md#security-grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace), [`security/no-runtime-grant`](security.md#security-no-runtime-grant).</sub>

<a id="security-process-exec-capability"></a>

## Running a program needs `process.exec` in server work, and there is no shell to interpolate into

`rule:security/process-exec-capability`

Running another program is a capability, `process.exec`, asked at the door
([`security/capability-check-at-the-door`](security.md#security-capability-check-at-the-door)). **A CLI run may run any program** when the key is not
written, as a command-line program in any other language does. **Server work runs no program**
without a written line. A written `exec` list replaces the default on both kinds of run, and `[]`
grants nothing. A request may narrow the grant further and never widen it, and calling without it
throws ([`security/denial-is-a-runtime-error`](security.md#security-denial-is-a-runtime-error)). The grant is asked for before the target is
looked at, so an ungranted deployment never learns whether a binary exists.

The capability is only half of it, and the other half is that **there is no shell to interpolate
into**. An executable path and an argv array, with nothing in between that parses a command line,
removes the escaping question rather than answering it — which is a stronger guarantee than any amount
of quoting. Under the sink predicate the executable path is an instruction, so the path is the sink
([`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate)). The argv elements are no sink of their own, and they are still typed
plain `string`, so an argument list holding a `tainted string` does not compile
([`core-classes/process-is-argv-only`](core-classes.md#core-classes-process-is-argv-only)): no shell parses an argument, but the program that receives
it does, and an attacker's value in that position can be an option such as `--output=/etc/passwd`.

A grant that names executable roots resolves the same way a spawn root does, canonicalise-then-prefix
([`security/path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix`](security.md#security-path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix)).

**A bare name such as `git` is looked up on `PATH`.** A bare name has no separator, no drive, and is
not `.` or `..`. The compiler leaves a bare name written as the program argument as it is, and joins
every other relative literal to its file's folder ([`programs/relative-paths-resolve-from-their-file`](programs.md#programs-relative-paths-resolve-from-their-file)).
At the door the lookup comes after the grant: a run whose grant allows no program at all is refused
before `PATH` is read. The program found is then asked about by its absolute path, like any other, so
the file the operating system starts is the file the check approved. Any other path that does not
start at a root is refused.

**A bare name in the grant is looked up on `PATH` once, when the configuration loads**, and the entry
becomes that program's absolute path. A name no folder of `PATH` answers is a load error that names
the entry. So `exec = ["git"]` in server work allows exactly the `git` the server would start. A
folder beside the configuration file is written with a separator, `"bin/"` or `"./bin"`.

**Cost:** one `stat` per folder of `PATH` per bare-name call, and the same per bare-name entry at load.

Declined:

- **A bare name resolved against the current directory.** Under `nvs serve` that directory is shared
  by every app and is a system folder under a service manager, so the name would start a different
  file depending on how the server was started.
- **A bare name looked up in server work before any grant exists.** The lookup would tell an
  ungranted deployment which programs are installed.
- **Programs open by default in server work.** A request that reaches any program reaches everything
  the server's user can run, which is the one thing a server most needs to keep closed.

<sub>See also [`security/capability-check-at-the-door`](security.md#security-capability-check-at-the-door), [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`security/script-spawn-capability`](security.md#security-script-spawn-capability), [`core-classes/process-is-argv-only`](core-classes.md#core-classes-process-is-argv-only), [`core-classes/process-refuses-a-shell-target`](core-classes.md#core-classes-process-refuses-a-shell-target).</sub>

<a id="security-net-address-policy"></a>

## `net.connect` carries an address policy that denies the private ranges, and an exception is one written IP address

`rule:security/net-address-policy`

`net.connect` is not a boolean and not merely a host list. It carries an address policy enforced on
**every outbound connection whose address the program supplies**, hardcoded URLs included, because a
hardcoded hostname can resolve into a private range and because deployment configuration supplies most
real endpoint URLs.

Denied by default: every address that is not globally routable. That is loopback, the private ranges,
**link-local**, unspecified, shared address space (`100.64.0.0/10`), protocol assignments
(`192.0.0.0/24`), benchmarking (`198.18.0.0/15`), multicast (`224.0.0.0/4`, `ff00::/8`), reserved
(`240.0.0.0/4`), broadcast, IPv6 site-local (`fec0::/10`) and the local-use NAT64 prefix
(`64:ff9b:1::/48`). That prefix is denied whole, because RFC 6052 lets its translator carry an IPv4
address in any of six layouts and the layout is the translator's setting, so no reading of an address
says which IPv4 address it reaches; an operator who runs one writes the prefix in `net.internal`. It is also every IPv6 form that carries one of those IPv4 addresses,
each of which reaches the address it carries: IPv4-mapped (`::ffff:0:0/96`), IPv4-compatible
(`::/96`), the NAT64 well-known prefix (`64:ff9b::/96`), 6to4 (`2002::/16`, the 32 bits after the
prefix) and Teredo (`2001::/32`, the inverted low 32 bits). The documentation ranges (`192.0.2.0/24`,
`198.51.100.0/24`, `203.0.113.0/24`, `2001:db8::/32`) are not denied: nothing routes them, so a
connection to one fails on its own. An operator grants an exception in `net.internal` as an **IP
address or a CIDR range written out** (`10.0.0.5`, `172.18.0.0/16`): a container network or a subnet
the operator runs is a range, and no list of addresses can follow it. Two things it is not, each a
widening this refuses: not a hostname, because the policy is asked of a resolved address and a name
would except whatever it resolved to afterwards; and not `true`, which is the one place a capability's
`true` does not mean everything. A range with bits set below its prefix (`10.0.0.5/8`) reads as one
host and would grant a block, so it is refused at load with the hostname and `true`.

**The application's own code reaches every public host by default**, on a CLI run and in server work,
so an unwritten `connect` is every host and the table above is the whole policy. A written `connect`
list narrows that to an allowlist. **Loopback (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`) is excepted by default on a CLI
run and in server work whose configuration names `development`.** That default is a startup row
([`config/a-startup-default-is-never-flipped`](config.md#config-a-startup-default-is-never-flipped)), so a program that flips itself to `development`
gains nothing, and a production server reaches loopback only where `internal` names it. A written
`internal` list replaces the default whole.

Link-local is the range whose omission is catastrophic rather than regrettable: `169.254.169.254` is the
cloud instance-metadata endpoint, and reaching it turns a feature that fetches a URL into credential
theft. The exception and the connect grant are independent and both required — `net.internal` reaches
nothing a written `net.connect` list does not name — so an exception is a second thing an operator
writes, not a way around the first. A production deployment that calls internal services has to say
so, and that is the point: the difference between an intended internal call and a forged one is
whether somebody wrote it down.

The one class of address it does not govern is an endpoint an operator wrote into root-owned
configuration and granted by name — that address is not attacker-influenceable, and applying the
policy there would deny every ordinary deployment. A program-supplied target stays governed in full.

A configured forward proxy is such an endpoint and is not asked the table's question; and under
`[http.client.proxy] resolve = "proxy"` the destination's resolved address is not asked it either,
because Novis never sees one — [`http-server/a-proxied-call-keeps-its-pin-unless-the-operator-says-otherwise`](http-server.md#http-server-a-proxied-call-keeps-its-pin-unless-the-operator-says-otherwise)
is where the operator writes that word and what the boot says every time they have.

"Connection" here means every outbound destination, not only a connected stream: a `Core\Net` datagram
sent to an address the program supplied is asked the same question at the send that a TCP connect is
asked at the connect. What the table does **not** govern is a *bind*, whose terms invert —
[`security/net-listen-is-a-separate-grant-from-net-connect`](security.md#security-net-listen-is-a-separate-grant-from-net-connect) is that grant and says why it carries
no policy of its own.

**Declined:**
- **Reading `64:ff9b:1::/48` as the IPv4 address in its low 32 bits**, as the well-known prefix is
  read. A translator set to a `/64` layout puts the address elsewhere, so a private address written
  that way reads as a public one. Denying the prefix costs an IPv6-only network that uses it one
  `net.internal` line.
- **No exception syntax at all**, so a private range is never reachable from a program-supplied
  address. Service-to-service calls are the normal case in any non-trivial deployment, and a rule that
  has to be worked around is worse than one that has to be written down.
- **The policy applied to an operator-written endpoint too.** A database or a shared store lives at a
  private address, a container network or loopback, so every ordinary deployment would be denied
  ([`core-classes/db-capabilities`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-capabilities), [`config/cache-shared-is-the-grant-over-the-configured-store`](config.md#config-cache-shared-is-the-grant-over-the-configured-store)).
- **Loopback always allowed, a production server included.** It would give up SSRF protection for
  every service listening on the machine, such as an admin port or an unauthenticated store, to save a
  production deployment one line.

<sub>See also [`security/outbound-url-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-outbound-url-is-a-sink), [`http-server/a-proxied-call-keeps-its-pin-unless-the-operator-says-otherwise`](http-server.md#http-server-a-proxied-call-keeps-its-pin-unless-the-operator-says-otherwise), [`security/the-policy-lives-in-the-capability`](security.md#security-the-policy-lives-in-the-capability), [`security/capability-question-is-grant-and-scope`](security.md#security-capability-question-is-grant-and-scope), [`security/net-listen-is-a-separate-grant-from-net-connect`](security.md#security-net-listen-is-a-separate-grant-from-net-connect), [`core-classes/db-capabilities`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-capabilities).</sub>

<a id="security-net-listen-is-a-separate-grant-from-net-connect"></a>

## The grant follows what the program is doing rather than the transport: reaching out is `net.connect`, binding is `net.listen`, and neither widens the other

`rule:security/net-listen-is-a-separate-grant-from-net-connect`

Which network capability an opening asks is decided by **what the program is doing**, not by which
transport it does it over. Reaching outward is `net.connect`, asked at `Scope::Host` and carrying
[`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy)'s denied-range table. Binding an endpoint is `net.listen`, asked of
the endpoint and carrying no address policy. Opening or binding a socket path is `net.local`
([`config/net-local-is-named-and-not-on-the-roster`](config.md#config-net-local-is-named-and-not-on-the-roster)). **None of the three widens either of the
others**: a program that may reach a host may not bind one, and a program that may open a local socket
may not reach the network.

One socket can need two of them, because it does two things. A `Core\Net` datagram socket asks
`net.listen` once for its local port and `net.connect` for **every destination it sends to**, resolved
and checked at the send exactly as a TCP connect is checked at the connect. Granting it once at the
bind instead would make UDP a way around the address policy entirely: a program holding only its own
port could send to any address in any denied range.

`net.listen`'s entries are `address:port` literals matched exactly, and `true` is "any endpoint this
process may bind". There is no denied-range table here because the policy's terms **invert** under a
bind: binding loopback is the contained case and binding the unspecified address is the exposed one,
so importing the outbound table would deny the safe spelling and permit the dangerous one. What a bind
actually risks — occupying a port another service expects, or exposing a surface to a network the
operator did not intend — is answered by naming the endpoint rather than by classifying its range.
Exact matching rather than a pattern or a port range is `net.internal`'s choice for `net.internal`'s
reason: an operator writing a range hands back more than the endpoint they meant, and the grant's
value is that a reviewer can see what a deployment opened. An entry that does not parse as an endpoint
matches nothing.

Three grants are three keys, and that is a real cost: an operator whose program binds writes
`net.listen` beside `net.connect`, and a reviewer reads both. It buys the property the roster exists
for, a grant that says one thing. A refusal names the grant that was missing and what was asked for:
the endpoint for `net.listen`, the canonical path for `net.local`, and for `net.connect` either the
ungranted host or the denied address it resolved to. A datagram refused at its destination is refused
at the send, not at the open.

A datagram's check at each send is a resolution on a hot path, the same one a TCP connect pays once.
If a datagram-heavy program shows it dominating, the answer is a pin cached on the socket for as long
as the destination is unchanged, never a grant asked once at the bind.

**Declined:**
- **`net.connect` widened to cover binds and socket paths.** One name would cover three guarantees,
  an operator granting an outbound host would silently grant a listener, and the address table it
  carries would be wrong for two of the three.
- **A datagram socket granted once, at the bind.** It makes UDP a way around the address policy.
- **A denied-range table for `net.listen`, inverted so that public addresses are denied.** It reads
  as symmetry and is a second policy to keep in step with the first, for a risk that naming the
  endpoint already answers exactly.

<sub>See also [`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy), [`config/net-local-is-named-and-not-on-the-roster`](config.md#config-net-local-is-named-and-not-on-the-roster), [`security/capability-roster-is-closed`](security.md#security-capability-roster-is-closed), [`core-classes/net-one-api-three-transports`](core-classes.md#core-classes-net-one-api-three-transports).</sub>

<a id="security-the-policy-lives-in-the-capability"></a>

## The address policy lives in the capability, so every client obeys it and none of them may hold its own

`rule:security/the-policy-lives-in-the-capability`

Every client — the HTTP client, the raw socket layer, a program-supplied database target, and any
socket a host import hands to an extension — is subject to the same policy, enforced at the point the
connection is made rather than inside any one of them.

A policy held by a client is a policy the next client does not have. Putting it in the capability
means an extension cannot be granted a socket that escapes it, which matters because an extension may
legitimately be an I/O source and several network clients sit outside the standard library. It also
means the answer to "what may this deployment reach" is one grant an operator reads, not a survey of
every class that opens a connection.

The exception is the same one [`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy) names — a config-named endpoint the
operator has already approved by writing it — and it is a property of the address, not of the client
that dials it.

<sub>See also [`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy), [`security/capability-check-at-the-door`](security.md#security-capability-check-at-the-door), [`security/outbound-url-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-outbound-url-is-a-sink).</sub>

<a id="security-tainted-qualifier"></a>

## `tainted` is a compile-time qualifier on `string`, `bytes` and a shape of them, spellable in any declaration and erased before codegen

`rule:security/tainted-qualifier`

`tainted string` and `tainted bytes` join the type grammar as a qualified form of the two scalar
types, and `tainted {…}` writes the same fact over a whole shape of them. It is not a class, not a
wrapper and not a run-time tag: it is checked once, while checking, and carries no representation past
that point — no extra byte in the value's header, no refcount change, nothing on the hot path.

**Over a shape it distributes and then disappears.** `tainted {a: string, b: {c: bytes}}` is rewritten
while parsing to the shape whose text-carrying fields are their tainted forms, transitively — through a
nested shape, a nullable, a union member and an `array<string>` element — so it produces exactly the
field-by-field spelling it saves, and no layer past the parser knows it was written. A shape carrying no
`string` and no `bytes` anywhere is a diagnostic rather than a no-op: a qualifier that promises nothing
still reads as a promise.

**`mixed` is not qualifiable, and that is the same boundary.** The checker cannot distribute a qualifier
through an erased container, so `tainted mixed` would promise what nothing enforces; structured input
stays `array<mixed>`. The qualifier is recovered where the payload is named instead: text out of `mixed`
is `tainted` however it is taken out ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)), and a request body converted
into a shape is converted into `tainted {…}` — not by qualifying the container it arrived in.

**It is grammar, not only a type-checker fact.** Every binding carries a written type
([`types/declaration`](types.md#types-declaration)), so a function that receives a tainted value and passes it on has nowhere
to put that fact unless `tainted` can be spelled in an ordinary declaration. Without it, taint would
disappear silently at the first call boundary — which is the hole the qualifier exists to close — or
every request-handling function would have to launder on its first line.

`tainted` is written after `secret` when both appear, and `tainted secret string` is a diagnostic
naming the required order rather than a second spelling ([`security/secret-qualifier`](security.md#security-secret-qualifier)).

**False positives are the accepted failure direction.** A value the program wrote itself can read back
`tainted` once it round-trips through a store, and [`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted) exists for that case
at the cost of one written reason per call site.

**Declined:**
- **Run-time taint tracking**, a tag carried on each value. It pays a representation and a per-operation
  cost on the request path for a guarantee the checker gives for nothing, and it finds a leak only when
  a test happens to drive the value into the sink.
- **A separate analysis pass beside the checker.** An optional pass can be skipped or silenced, and that
  is not the guarantee of a checker that refuses to compile the program.
- **Tainting a shape hydrated from a request on its own**, without `tainted {…}` written. The
  declaration would then understate the value, and a type that is not what it says is worse than a
  long one.
- **Writing `tainted` on each field of a request shape by hand, as the only form.** It is correct but
  long enough that programs stop writing it, and [`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources) is only worth as much
  as the declarations that carry it forward.

<sub>See also [`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources), [`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation), [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`types/grammar`](types.md#types-grammar).</sub>

<a id="security-tainted-sources"></a>

## Every accessor that hands a program bytes from outside answers the `tainted` form, and the list of them is enumerable

`rule:security/tainted-sources`

Every member of the request, server, session, environment and CLI accessors, and a script's own
arguments, answers the `tainted` form of whatever it already returned. Header values and any other
client-influenced field are included; a fixed enum-shaped field such as the request method is not
attacker-shaped in the same way and is not required to be.

**An outbound reply's body is input in the same sense**, so a response body read back from a client
answers `tainted string`: pinning an address settles which host the bytes came from and says nothing
about what is in them, and a reply a program asked for is no safer than one it was sent. Its status
code is not tainted — three digits carry nothing a sink can misread. Values read back out of a
database are `tainted` under the same standing rule, which is what closes stored injection by the same
mechanism as reflected.

**An object read from storage is `tainted` too.** `Core\Storage::get` answers `?tainted bytes`: a
disk is where a program puts what a visitor uploaded, so an object is a row by another name.
`Core\Storage::list` answers plain keys, since a key is one to 255 letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_`,
and like a status code it carries nothing a sink can misread. **A file read through `Core\IO` is not
`tainted`.** Most such reads are the program's own templates, data and assets, and a program that
keeps uploads as plain files chose the folder an upload lands in. An upload itself is `tainted` where
it enters, through `Core\Request\Part`.

**A request field is read as text, and typed at the accessor.** `Core\Request::query` and `::post`
answer one field as `?tainted string` — `null` for a name that is absent and for one written with
brackets — and `::queryArray` and `::postArray` answer a bracketed name's one level of values as
`array<tainted string>`, keyed as the brackets keyed them — so a `foreach` key over one is `tainted
string` as well ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)) — refusing a second level with a `ParseError`
that names `queryAs`/`postAs`. A deeper shape is those two members' to validate into a written type,
so no request accessor answers a field as `mixed`. A value that is `mixed` by nature — a decoded
document such as `json()`, a session or cache entry, a row's `get` — carries the qualifier the moment
text is pulled out of it, because text out of `mixed` is `tainted` ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)).
A typed reader answers the tainted form itself: a row's `string` is `?tainted string` and its `bytes`
is `?tainted bytes`. The list of sources being **enumerable** is what lets the qualifier attach itself
automatically, and is exactly what `secret` has no equivalent of
([`security/secret-has-no-ambient-source`](security.md#security-secret-has-no-ambient-source)).

**`Core\Env::secret` is the environment's one read that is not `tainted`.** It answers `?secret
string` ([`security/secret-has-no-ambient-source`](security.md#security-secret-has-no-ambient-source)). `tainted` stops a value at a sink that would
read it as an instruction: a URL, a path, a query, markup. A `secret` reaches none of those, because
every output and instruction sink already refuses it, and it does reach the two places a credential
belongs, an outbound header and a database password, which refuse `tainted`. Carrying both bits would
make the member unusable for its one purpose. The operator who started the process chose the value,
as they chose `nvs.toml`; `Core\Env::get` stays `tainted` because its value may reach any sink.

**`Core\Random\Seeded::bytes` answers `tainted bytes` and `::token` answers `tainted string`, and
every key parameter refuses `tainted`.** Anyone who knows the seed draws the same bytes again, so
they are as predictable as a visitor's text. A key parameter is a sink on the `tainted` axis: no
octet of a key reaches an answer, but a key somebody else chose or can predict protects nothing.
That covers each key `Core\Crypto`, `Core\Crypto\KeyPair::read`, `Core\Hash::hmac`, `Core\Csrf`,
`Core\Jwt`, `Core\Jwe\Key::shared` and `Core\Totp` take, and every key ring (`Core\SignedCookie`,
`Core\Signature`, the session and cache rings, signed URLs). A key a program stored in a database
row is `tainted` too, and reaches a key parameter through `Core\Taint::assertTrustedBytes` with its
reason. The seeded `int`, `float`, `pick`, `sample` and `shuffle` stay plain: none is the type a key
parameter takes. `nvs_stdlib::keyring::KEY` is the one type every key parameter is written with.

No `Core` member names a qualifier, and the taint diagnosis has no opt-out. A `taintedPostAs` would
make every other member's name read as a claim it does not make. A caller who finds the diagnosis
verbose writes `tainted {…}` over the shape.

**Declined:**
- **A `predictable` qualifier of its own.** It would be a third axis that every signature and every
  diagnostic carries, for one source. `tainted` already says "do not let this decide anything".
- **Every `Core\IO` read answering `tainted`.** Each template, fixture and shipped data file would
  need `Core\Taint::assertTrusted` with a reason, and the reason would be the same everywhere. A
  qualifier written that often stops being read. A program that stores uploads should use
  `Core\Storage`, whose reads are `tainted`.
- **A run-time check that a key looks random.** No test of a 32-byte buffer tells a seeded draw from
  a real one.

<sub>See also [`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier), [`security/secret-has-no-ambient-source`](security.md#security-secret-has-no-ambient-source), [`statements/no-host-populated-variables`](statements.md#statements-no-host-populated-variables).</sub>

<a id="security-taint-propagation"></a>

## A tainted operand poisons every operation it takes part in, and only a checked conversion launders for free

`rule:security/taint-propagation`

Any operation combining a tainted operand with an untainted one — concatenation, interpolation, a
string member, an array of scalars — produces a tainted result. This is the poisoned shape the type
system already uses on other axes, applied to a new one, and `secret` poisons independently beside it
([`security/secret-propagation`](security.md#security-secret-propagation)).

**An encoder's result carries the text it encodes.** `Core\Json::encode` and `Core\Serialize::encode`
write every string of the value they walk into their result — JSON escaping leaves a `'` where it was,
and `decode` rebuilds every object of the graph — so the result is `tainted string` or `tainted bytes`
when the value carries outside text anywhere:
a tainted atom, or `mixed`, `object`, `iterable` or an unresolved type parameter, at any depth of an
array, a shape or an object's properties. An object is read through every class it can be at run
time, the declared class and each concrete class extending or implementing it. A value that provably
carries none — an `array<int>`, a shape or an object whose fields are all clean, an array literal of
the program's own values — encodes to the plain type. `Core\Uri::buildQuery` and
`Core\Uri::withQueryParameter` percent-encode every byte that is not safe in a URL, as `encodeFormValue`
does, and answer the plain type for that launderer's reason. `Core\Str::format` and `Core\Bytes::pack`
are encoders of their variadic arguments by the same rule: the template is a sink, and a `%s` filled
from outside text makes the result `tainted`.

**No `Core` signature loses a mark.** `crates/nvs-stdlib/tests/taint_signatures.rs` reads every row,
and fails naming each member that answers a plain `string` or `bytes`, or hands its callback one,
while a parameter could carry outside text the row does not classify: an array, `mixed`, `object` or a
type variable. Its allow list is the encoders above and the launderers
([`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named)), each with the rule that makes it one.

**Text out of `mixed` is `tainted`.** `mixed` is where request input lands and the qualifier cannot be
written on it ([`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier)), so every way text leaves it adds the bit: `as string`
and `as ?string` answer `tainted string` and `?tainted string`, `as bytes` answers `tainted bytes`,
`as array<string>` answers `array<tainted string>`, `as secret string` answers `secret tainted string`,
and a `.` or an interpolation with a `mixed` operand is tainted. `$m is string` narrows `$m` to
`tainted string` on the true edge, and over a `mixed` subject `is tainted {…}` and `is tainted string`
are admitted. The same holds for an `array<mixed>` operand and for a union with a `mixed` member.
So a member that answers `mixed` or `array<mixed>` accepts `tainted` text where its parameter is
contagious: `Core\Json::decode` of a `tainted string` answers `mixed`, and the mark is on each
string read out of it.
**The keys of such a value are outside text too**: a `foreach` key over a `mixed` or `iterable`
subject, or over an array whose element type carries `tainted` or `mixed` anywhere — `queryArray`,
`postArray`, `headers()`, a decoded `array<mixed>` — is `tainted string`, because an array's type says
nothing of its keys and its elements are the evidence of where it was filled. A `Core\Arr` member that
returns a key, or hands one to its callback, follows the same test: `keys`, `firstKey`, `lastKey`,
`keyOf` and `findKey` over such an array answer `tainted string`, and so does the `$key` of a `map`,
`filter` or `reduce` callback. Every member that fills
an array from outside answers one with such elements, so the element type covers members not yet
written too. An array the program fills with tainted values under its own literal keys over-taints,
which is the safe direction: write `tainted string $k`, and bind or escape the key where it reaches a
sink. The bound is a map nested in a decoded target: a `postAs<Form>` whose `Form` has an `array<int>`
field is keyed by the peer and has clean elements, so its keys bind as plain `string`. An object's fields are
read the same way: a shape target of `as` or `is` over a class takes each text field from the field of
that name, so a field that is `mixed`, `object` or tainted, or one the class does not declare and only
a subclass could, counts as outside text. Where the text would land in a type the program *wrote* — a
shape target of `as` or `is` over a `mixed` or `object` operand or over such an object, or a `foreach`
key or value binding — the qualifier is never added behind the declaration: a field or binding written
without `tainted` is a diagnostic asking for `tainted {…}` or `tainted string` (`E0851`), and a `var`
key takes `tainted string` itself. `object` counts with `mixed` for a shape target because its fields
are as untyped as `mixed`'s, so `$m as object` is no step round the rule. A shape target whose
qualified fields are all `tainted` is admitted by `as`, and over an unchecked subject by `is`, and is
tested with the qualifier erased; a `secret` field stays refused. A literal that was stored in `mixed`
and is genuinely trusted, or the text of a `Stringable` object pulled out of one, is recovered with
[`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted), or with the sink's own launderer.

**A key from outside enters only an array whose keys read back tainted.** Since the element type is
the only evidence, `$m[$key] = …` with a `tainted` key into an array whose element type carries
neither `tainted` nor `mixed` is `E0401` at the key. So are `??=`, every compound write, a nested
level such as `$m[$key]["n"] = …`, and a literal's `[$key => …]` against its declared or inferred type.
`unset` adds no key and is not checked. The cost is an update to a key already there, such as a count
per status read from a row: the checker cannot see that the key exists, so the program compares the
text with its own keys and writes through the matching one, or passes the key through
[`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted).

The rule sits at the one boundary every `mixed` source shares — `Core\Request::json`,
`Core\Script::args`, `Core\Session::get`, `Core\Json::decode`, `Core\Cache::get`, a row's `get`,
`Core\Serialize::decode`, `Core\Uri::queryParameter`, a socket's or event stream's `value` — so it
covers members not yet written as well.

A checked `as` conversion to a type that already throws on a malformed shape — `as uint`, `as int`,
`as float`, `as bool`, an enum's backing type, a set of allowed values — **removes the qualifier on
success**, from a tainted operand and from a `mixed` one alike. No new syntax is needed: a value that
survived the check has had its shape proven, which is what laundering means for a non-string type.
`as ?T` decides the qualifier by exactly this rule and launders nothing of its own
([`expressions/conversion-keeps-qualifiers`](expressions.md#expressions-conversion-keeps-qualifiers)).

`bytes as string` and `string as bytes` **preserve** the qualifier in either direction, and so does a
conversion out of a `?tainted string` or an `array<tainted string>`. UTF-8 validity says nothing about
whether the content is safe for a given sink, and a conversion that laundered here would be a one-word
bypass of every rule below. All of it is decided while checking: no tag at run time, nothing on the
request path.

- **Memory:** none. The qualifier is erased before codegen; the cost is compile time, one walk of the
  operand's type per conversion, `.`, interpolation and type test, one walk of the subject's element
  type per `foreach` with a key, and one property lookup per text field of a shape target over an
  object.

**Declined:**
- **Typed request accessors as the only fix.** They leave `json()`, `Core\Script::args`,
  `Core\Session::get`, `Core\Cache::get` and a row's `get` open, and every later member answering
  `mixed` would reopen the gap.
- **A hidden, source-marked `mixed`** carrying an invisible "came from outside" bit. It is lost at the
  first `mixed` parameter or property, it cannot be written in a declaration, and `tainted mixed` is
  refused for the same reason ([`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier)).
- **A key qualifier on the array type**, such as `array<tainted string => T>`, set by the members
  that fill an array from outside. It is exact, and it closes the nested-map bound above, but it adds
  a type parameter to every array and a second axis to assignability, which simplicity does not buy
  until that shape turns up in practice. A write with a `tainted` key into a plain-keyed array is
  refused instead, which keeps the element type's evidence true.
- **Letting a `tainted` key through when it updates a key that is already there.** Whether it is
  there is a run-time fact, so the checker would have to trust an `Core\Arr::hasKey` test that the
  next statement can invalidate.
- **Tainting a written shape target or binding without `tainted` written.** The declaration would then
  understate the value, and a type that is not what it says is worse than a long one.
- **Refusing `as string` out of `mixed` outright.** It leaves no way to read text from a request at
  all, and the tainted result is exactly what a sink needs to see.

<sub>See also [`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier), [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion), [`expressions/conversion-keeps-qualifiers`](expressions.md#expressions-conversion-keeps-qualifiers).</sub>

<a id="security-sink-predicate"></a>

## A `string` or `bytes` parameter is a sink when its content becomes an instruction a parser executes

`rule:security/sink-predicate`

> A `string`/`bytes` parameter is a `tainted` sink when its content becomes an instruction that a
> parser executes. It is not a sink when its content is data that a parser returns, or that a
> serializer or a protocol frames.

That one line derives every worked case, which is the test of it being the right predicate rather than
a restatement. A query's text is a sink and its bound parameters are not, because the wire protocol
frames each value. An argv element is data *because* there is no shell to execute it, while the
executable path is an instruction. A header value is a sink because `CR`/`LF` re-frames the message; a
body is not, because `Content-Length` frames it. A path component is a sink because `..` and
separators direct the resolver; a file's contents are not. A regex pattern is a sink; its subject is
not.

A new sink therefore needs no rule of its own — it needs the predicate applied. The four
grammars the library parses are all instructions by it
([`security/every-grammar-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-every-grammar-is-a-sink)), and a member nobody classified fails closed
([`security/unclassified-parameter-refuses-tainted`](security.md#security-unclassified-parameter-refuses-tainted)).

**Declined:**
- **Denying `tainted` at the process boundary, so it may leave only through a typed carrier.** Strictly
  stronger and wrong: it refuses a file's contents, an outbound request body, a bound database parameter
  and a log field, each of which is safe and common. The predicate is what separates them, so a boundary
  rule would be this rule with its useful half deleted.

<sub>See also [`security/unclassified-parameter-refuses-tainted`](security.md#security-unclassified-parameter-refuses-tainted), [`security/log-is-not-a-sink`](security.md#security-log-is-not-a-sink), [`security/every-grammar-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-every-grammar-is-a-sink), [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`core-classes/db-parameters`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-parameters).</sub>

<a id="security-unclassified-parameter-refuses-tainted"></a>

## A `Core` parameter nobody classified refuses a tainted argument, and refuses to ship at all

`rule:security/unclassified-parameter-refuses-tainted`

A `Core` member whose `string`/`bytes` parameter carries no classification **rejects a tainted
argument**. *Contagious* is a thing an author writes rather than a thing an author gets by forgetting,
and the failure direction inverts: before, a member nobody classified accepted tainted data at run
time in production; now it refuses where the call is written.

The classification lives once, beside the parameter list and the return type in the member registry,
and a member with an unclassified parameter **fails the library's own test suite** — the default is
what a program sees, the test is what stops such a member from shipping at all. Userland was already
fail-closed, because a plain `string` parameter of a user's function refuses a tainted argument, so the
library's own table was the one fail-open surface, and flipping its default was one pass over one table
rather than a language change. The pass marks most parameters *contagious*, because most genuinely
are, and it never recurs: the next member added is safe until its author says otherwise.

Every mark is checked before the program runs and erased before code is generated, so the default
costs nothing on the request path: no representation, no branch.

A **union parameter** carries the mark its arms declare — `Pattern|string` is a sink because the
`string` arm is written as one — and carries none where its arms disagree or where an arm that could
hold a mark does not. The classification is still written once beside the parameter, on the arm that
has a cell for it, and the refusing default still covers everything nobody classified.

A mark that admits `tainted` admits a union carrying it, arm by arm, and the contagion is read back
out with at least that reach. `Core\Env::get` returns `?tainted string`, so `$name ?? "default"` is a
`string|tainted string`, and that is the shape every environment read arrives in: a launderer that
took only the atom would refuse the one form its own source produces. The admission does not weaken,
because each arm is narrowed and then compared, so one tainted arm at a sink still refuses the whole
union. The two directions are deliberately asymmetric: the answer that decides
whether to *set* the qualifier on a result reaches further than the narrowing that decides whether to
*admit* an argument, because reaching too far over-taints in the first case and leaks in the second.

**Declined:**
- **Keeping *contagious* as the default and stating the sink predicate as guidance.** The predicate was
  already derivable, and a member taking a format template was still added unmarked. A rule held by
  attention fails exactly when nobody is paying it.

<sub>See also [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier), [`testing/capability-completeness-test`](testing.md#testing-capability-completeness-test).</sub>

<a id="security-every-grammar-is-a-sink"></a>

## Every grammar the library parses is a sink, and none of the four gets a launderer

`rule:security/every-grammar-is-a-sink`

The library parses exactly four grammars — a regex pattern, a format template, a date pattern, and a
byte-packing format — and every one of them is an instruction under [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate).
So each of the four is a sink, and the count that fixes the library's grammar surface doubles as the
roster.

**A regex replacement is a sink too.** It is not a grammar of its own under
[`core-api/no-mode-strings`](core-api.md#core-api-no-mode-strings), since it belongs to one member, but `Core\Regex::replace` reads `$1`,
`${name}` and `$$` in it, so a `tainted` one would let the request choose which captured text lands
where. Text from
outside goes into a result through `Core\Regex::replaceWith`, whose function returns it as text and
never reads it as a template.

**An XML processing instruction is a sink for the same reason, though it is written rather than
parsed.** `Core\Xml\Writer::instruction` escapes nothing, since XML has no escape inside one, and its
data is an instruction to the program that reads the document: an `xml-stylesheet` names the file a
browser fetches and runs. Its target and data refuse `tainted`; the writer's text, attribute, comment
and CDATA members escape or refuse what they cannot write, and stay launderers.

**No launderer is added for any of them, deliberately.** A grammar is written by the program, not
received by it, so the fix at a failing call site is to use a literal — which is folded at compile time
for all four ([`expressions/intrinsic-constant-arguments`](expressions.md#expressions-intrinsic-constant-arguments)) — or,
for a genuinely dynamic template drawn from a translation catalogue, [`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted) with
its written reason.

A regex quoting member remains the one exception on the roster, because a regex is the one grammar
that routinely needs a runtime value *inside* it rather than *as* it
([`security/regex-pattern-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-regex-pattern-is-a-sink)).

**Declined:**
- **A replacement option that reads the text literally.** `replaceWith` already inserts text as it is,
  and an option would be a second way to write one thing.

<sub>See also [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`security/regex-pattern-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-regex-pattern-is-a-sink), [`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted), [`expressions/intrinsic-constant-arguments`](expressions.md#expressions-intrinsic-constant-arguments).</sub>

<a id="security-regex-pattern-is-a-sink"></a>

## A regex pattern is a sink with no launderer; the subject is data and may be tainted

`rule:security/regex-pattern-is-a-sink`

A regex **pattern** requires the plain, unqualified `string`. A user-supplied pattern is both a
denial-of-service vector and a logic-injection vector: a pattern an attacker controls can be made to
match anything, which turns a validation check into an approval.

**There is no laundering member for it**, because there is no meaningful way to make an arbitrary
attacker-authored pattern safe. A program that genuinely needs one uses
[`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted) and says why. That is the shape every grammar on the roster takes
([`security/every-grammar-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-every-grammar-is-a-sink)); the regex quoting member is not a counter-example, because
it escapes a value to sit *inside* a pattern rather than to *be* one.

The **subject** may be tainted, and contagion applies unchanged: a substring matched out of a tainted
subject is tainted ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)). The denial-of-service half is answered
separately, by tiering the pattern onto a linear-time engine and budgeting the backtracking tier.

<sub>See also [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`security/every-grammar-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-every-grammar-is-a-sink), [`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted), [`core-classes/regex-two-tiers`](core-classes.md#core-classes-regex-two-tiers).</sub>

<a id="security-outbound-url-is-a-sink"></a>

## An outbound URL or address is a sink, and a tainted one is refused where it is written

`rule:security/outbound-url-is-a-sink`

The URL parameter of an HTTP client's request members, and the address parameter of a raw connect, are
unqualified: a `tainted` value at either position is a compile-time diagnostic, exactly as at a query
text parameter. Server-side request forgery starts with an attacker-chosen address, and this is the
position where that is visible.

The plain form covers URLs the program itself authored — a literal, a configuration value, a composed
path — and a literal is additionally validated while checking
([`expressions/intrinsic-constant-arguments`](expressions.md#expressions-intrinsic-constant-arguments)). A URL that genuinely came from outside goes through the
laundering member that also **pins** the address it resolved to, so the check and the connection
cannot disagree about which host was approved.

Refusing at the call site is only half of it: the address is judged again at run time against the
capability's own policy ([`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy)), because a hardcoded hostname can still
resolve into a private range.

Request forgery is an injection, but it is the one that cannot be settled at compile time alone: a
well-formed URL is harmless or not according to the address it resolves to, which is known only at
connect time and can differ between two resolutions of one name. Nor can it be settled at run time
alone, since nothing in the source would show a developer which URL is attacker-influenced. So it gets
both layers. Fetching a URL somebody supplied is a legitimate feature — webhooks, previews, imports — and
stays two lines, the second of which is the launderer that records the decision.

**Declined:**
- **The run-time policy alone, with no `tainted` refusal.** The developer gets no signal at `nvs check`
  and the failure appears in production, and this class alone would lose the compile-time audit every
  other injection has.
- **The compile-time refusal alone, with a launderer checking the URL's shape.** `http://169.254.169.254/`
  is well-formed, so the attack passes straight through.
- **A launderer answering a plain `string`.** It reopens the gap between the check and the connection
  ([`http-server/allow-url-pins-the-address`](http-server.md#http-server-allow-url-pins-the-address)).
- **Leaving it to the application, with documentation.** Every application re-implements it, most
  incompletely, and a language that makes SQL and HTML injection compile errors would be treating this one
  as a matter of care.

<sub>See also [`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy), [`security/the-policy-lives-in-the-capability`](security.md#security-the-policy-lives-in-the-capability), [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`expressions/intrinsic-constant-arguments`](expressions.md#expressions-intrinsic-constant-arguments).</sub>

<a id="security-metric-label-refuses-tainted"></a>

## A metric label value refuses `tainted`, and there is deliberately no launderer for one

`rule:security/metric-label-refuses-tainted`

A metric label value is a sink: a query parameter, a header, a path segment or a database column
cannot become a label.

There is deliberately **no launderer for it**, because there is no sanitisation that would make one
safe. The hazard is not the value's content, it is that the value is drawn from an unbounded set, and
an unbounded label set is how a metrics collector falls over. What exists instead is everything that
is already unqualified and is what a label should have been: an enum case or an integer converted with
`as`, which laundering makes free ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)); a route's path pattern from the
compiled table; a literal, a class constant or a configured value; and, for a genuinely bounded user-derived
set, [`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted).

`secret` is refused there too and needs no new rule: a metric export is output, and every output sink
already refuses it ([`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse)).

The cost is a compile error at exactly the line that would have taken the collector down, and it is
there because the qualifier system already exists for injection. Labelling by a user id, a tenant
name or an error message is what people reach for first, so this refusal is met often.

**Declined:**
- **Allowing `tainted` labels behind a runtime cardinality guard.** The guard fires after the
  collector already has the series, and a compile error at the responsible line is strictly better
  than a warning hours later on another machine.

<sub>See also [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted), [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type).</sub>

<a id="security-log-is-not-a-sink"></a>

## A log field is data, so it takes a tainted value and wants one

`rule:security/log-is-not-a-sink`

A log field is data: the writer is a structured serializer, so a field is framed by the serializer and
never by string concatenation into a line. Log forging is therefore closed by the writer's shape
([`errors/log-write`](errors.md#errors-log-write)), independently of the qualifier system, and logging tainted content is
*desired* rather than tolerated — recording exactly what an attacker sent is the point of a security
log.

The same holds for a bidirectional control, which the writer escapes by construction
([`security/bidi-boundaries`](security.md#security-bidi-boundaries)), and for a JSON decode, whose input is data the parse returns to the
program and whose result is `tainted`; its risk is bounded by the decoder's nesting cap, which is on
by default.

The `secret` axis does not follow: a log field **refuses** a `secret` value, because that axis is
about confidentiality rather than structure and a log is an output
([`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse)). Stating both here is what stops a future reader from applying
one rule's answer to the other axis.

<sub>See also [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse), [`errors/log-fields`](errors.md#errors-log-fields), [`errors/log-write`](errors.md#errors-log-write).</sub>

<a id="security-launderers-are-sink-named"></a>

## The only way out of `tainted` is a `Core` member whose contract names the one sink it is safe for

`rule:security/launderers-are-sink-named`

Short of a checked conversion, the only way to remove `tainted` is a `Core` member whose contract
states which **one** sink it is safe for: an HTML escape for HTML text, an identifier quote for a
dynamic table or column name, a path containment check for a path component, and one per sink as each
class is designed.

There is deliberately no generic `sanitize()` or `clean()`. A value safe for HTML text is not safe for
a shell argument or a path, and a single catch-all invites exactly the false confidence the qualifier
exists to prevent. The roster grows by adding a named member to the class that owns the sink, never by
widening an existing one.

**One launderer checks nothing in the bytes: `Core\Path::fromCwd`**, for a file path typed on the
command line. It throws while a request is being answered, so request data never passes through it.
The user who typed the path can already open any file the process can, and the `fs` grants still
bound every file its answer names. A request that opens a file named by its own data keeps
`Core\IO::within($base, $path)`. `fromCwd` removes `tainted` and nothing else: a `secret` argument
does not compile, as at every launderer. A queued job and a spawned isolate answer no request, so
`fromCwd` runs there whatever text they were handed, and that isolate's `fs` grants bound the file its
answer names. Without the exception, the one use the member exists for, a command-line tool opening
the file its user named, needs `Core\Taint::assertTrusted` at every call.

Which return type a launderer takes is a predicate rather than a per-member choice
([`security/launderer-answers-a-carrier`](security.md#security-launderer-answers-a-carrier)). Where no built-in launderer fits, the way out is
[`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted) — written, greppable, and carrying a reason — and never a silent cast.

**Declined:**

- **A new `CoreTy` for "a path from the command line".** It marks the same fact the qualifier already
  marks, and every path door would have to accept the new type.
- **Keeping `fromCwd`'s answer `tainted` and documenting `Core\Taint::assertTrusted`.** The greppable
  escape hatch becomes a line every command-line tool writes, so it stops marking the unusual call.
- **Laundering `Core\Cli::arguments` itself.** An argument is also a shell word, an SQL value and HTML
  text, and a launderer names one sink.

<sub>See also [`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted), [`security/launderer-answers-a-carrier`](security.md#security-launderer-answers-a-carrier), [`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation), [`core-classes/html-auto-escape`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-auto-escape).</sub>

<a id="security-launderer-answers-a-carrier"></a>

## A launderer answers its sink's carrier when that sink launders on its own and the transform is not idempotent, and a plain type otherwise

`rule:security/launderer-answers-a-carrier`

A `Core` member that removes `tainted` answers its sink's **carrier type** rather than the plain type
when **both** hold: its sink launders automatically — a value reaches that sink and is transformed
with no call written at the site — and its transform is **not idempotent**, so applying it to its own
output changes the output. Otherwise it answers the plain type.

The two conditions are one question asked twice: *a second application the source does not show, of a
transform a second application changes.* Only HTML output meets both today, which is why the HTML
escape answers a carrier and every other launderer on the roster — identifier quoting, URI component
and form-value encoding, regex quoting, terminal escaping — answers a `string`, by the predicate
rather than by exemption. Their results are legitimately concatenated into a larger string, and a
carrier would force a builder API onto four classes to close a hazard whose second call is already
visible in the source.

A launderer written for a *new* sink is measured against the two conditions, not against today's
table, and a sink that acquires an automatic launder reclassifies its own member the day it does.

**Why a `string` is the wrong answer at such a sink.** A `string` carries one bit where the domain has
three states: untrusted, plain text nobody has escaped, and already escaped for this sink. The second
and third are the same type, so an escaped value concatenated into tainted text is re-poisoned,
correctly, and the sink then escapes it a second time: `&` becomes `&amp;amp;` with no diagnostic
anywhere. With a carrier the three states are three types — `tainted string`, `string` and
`Core\Html\Markup` — and no operator moves a value backwards between them, so every ordering of a
concatenation is either correct or refused. Neither condition alone is a hazard: a non-idempotent
transform at a sink that never launders on its own takes a visible second call to break, and a
terminal escape is idempotent because its substitute contains no escape byte.

A registry guard holds it: the whole roster of launderers is listed with whether each answers a
carrier, so a launderer added in any class fails the guard until somebody places it against the
predicate.

**Memory:** nothing a program did not already spend. The sink's escape-and-lift makes a `Markup`
anyway, so a carrier answer removes the second escape rather than adding a wrapper.

**Declined:**
- **The HTML sink detects already-escaped text and skips it.** `&amp;` in the input is text that said
  `&amp;`, and it must come back as `&amp;amp;`; a sink that guesses is one an attacker can aim
  ([`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused)).
- **A third qualifier, `escaped string`.** New grammar, a new keyword and a third axis in the checker,
  to say what a carrier class already says for free.
- **A carrier for every non-idempotent launderer**, such as a URI component, a database identifier and
  a regex pattern type. It forces a builder API onto four classes whose values are normally assembled
  by concatenation, against a hazard that takes a visible second call to reach.

<sub>See also [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`security/capture-answers-the-carrier`](security.md#security-capture-answers-the-carrier), [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), [`core-classes/html-escape-answers-markup`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-escape-answers-markup), [`core-classes/html-to-source`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-to-source).</sub>

<a id="security-capture-answers-the-carrier"></a>

## Capturing a sink yields that sink's carrier, never a plain `string`

`rule:security/capture-answers-the-carrier`

Capturing output answers **the carrier of the sink in force**, not a plain `string`. The reason is not
symmetry: the captured bytes have *already* been through the sink, so handing them back as a `string`
and re-emitting them would escape them a second time and corrupt the page.

The same rule gives a spawned isolate's captured result its type
([`security/isolate-output-is-captured`](security.md#security-isolate-output-is-captured)), by the same argument and with the same fix. Inheriting
rather than capturing needs no rule at all: the child's carrier is the parent's, so appending composes
the way carrier addition already does.

**A body member's bytes pass the sink too, where they become a carrier.** `Core\Response::text`,
`::json`, `::bytes` and `::stream` write verbatim, because what they write is a response with its own
media type. Inside a capture, and in a `spawn script` child, it is not: it becomes the carrier, or is
appended to the parent's stream. There those four write as `echo` writes a `string`, escaped under the
HTML sink and substituted under every other, so a child's `text("<script>…")` shows as text in the
parent's page and an `echo`ed one is escaped once. Bytes that are not UTF-8 are rendered byte by
byte and still make a capture throw. `html` writes a `Markup` and `sendFile` a file the program
named, so both stay verbatim. The cost is one copy of such a body where the rendering changes it.
(`crates/nvs-runtime/src/ctx/output.rs`'s `a_body_that_becomes_markup_is_escaped_and_a_response_is_verbatim`,
`tests/hostile/lang/concurrency/isolates-spawn-script-and-await/02-a-child-writes-markup-the-parent-prints.nvs`.)

This is the third instance of one rule rather than three members that each argued it alone — the other
two being a laundering escape and an approved URL — and stating it once is what keeps a future
capturing member from answering the wrong type ([`security/launderer-answers-a-carrier`](security.md#security-launderer-answers-a-carrier)).

<sub>See also [`security/isolate-output-is-captured`](security.md#security-isolate-output-is-captured), [`security/launderer-answers-a-carrier`](security.md#security-launderer-answers-a-carrier), [`security/response-body-is-one-typed-member`](security.md#security-response-body-is-one-typed-member).</sub>

<a id="security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type"></a>

## A route capture is laundered by the parameter's own type, and a `string` capture stays tainted

`rule:security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`

Every capture in a route path corresponds to a parameter of the same name, and the parameter's
declared type is what the segment is converted to during matching. A failed conversion is **not a
match**: matching continues, and if nothing else matches the result is a 404 — which is what every
framework otherwise writes by hand as a digit constraint on the placeholder.

**A capture or a `#[Query]` parameter declared `bool`, `true` or `false` is `E0752`.** A segment is
text, and no spelling of a `bool` is the one a link would build and a match would read, so a `bool`
capture would match every segment and arrive as text. A command's `bool` option is a flag given by
being written, which is why the conversion list [`tooling/commands-are-compiled`](tooling.md#tooling-commands-are-compiled) shares with this
rule admits it there and not here.

**A capture typed at a class built from text is the one exception, and it fails the other way.** The
matcher narrows on the conversions it reads natively — `int`, `uint`, `decimal`, `Core\Uuid` and a
closed set — and a capture declared at any *other* class implementing `Parses` matches on **shape**.
Matching runs at the door with no program installed, so calling that class's `parse` there would put an
implementor's body over every request URL, including the ones that match no route, ahead of everything
that rate-limits it — the priority-1 objection this rule already makes to a regex, and a `parse` body is
strictly more than a regex. The class's `parse` runs at the binding site instead, where the match
crosses into the program, so a segment it refuses is a **`400`** over a route that did match rather than
a `404` ([`routing/a-bad-query-value-is-a-400`](routing.md#routing-a-bad-query-value-is-a-400)). Two captures spelled the same way therefore fail
two ways, and what decides which is who runs at the door. The refusal is the class's own throw and
travels unchanged, so a program that reads the match without a `catch` fails the request; a handler
that wants the non-throwing answer calls the class's `tryParse` ([`expressions/try-parse`](expressions.md#expressions-try-parse)). The
captures cross as `array<tainted string|int|uint|decimal|Core\Uuid|Parses>`, the last member an
interface because the set of classes it means is open.

**A converted capture arrives unqualified.** A checked conversion launders
([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)), so an integer or enum capture is a plain value, while a `string`
capture and a trailing-segment capture stay `tainted string`, because nothing about them was checked.
A capture at a class built from text arrives as an instance of that class, which carries no qualifier
because `tainted` is a property of `string` and `bytes` and never of a class
([`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier)) — an implementor that keeps the text in a plain `string` field is
refused by the assignability rule that already stands. No new sink, no new launderer, no new rule — the
existing one arriving somewhere useful.

**Memory:** a capture at a class built from text costs one call into the program on the matched route
and nowhere else, and its row holds one extra string, the class's name. `Core\Request::route()` takes
the match by clone, one reference-count bump on the row plus one string per capture. A request that
matches nothing pays nothing.

**Declined:**
- **Arming a class table at the door, so the matcher calls `parse`.** It keeps one failure mode for
  every capture, and puts an unbounded, application-authored body on the unauthenticated request path
  ahead of any rate limit.
- **Carrying a class-typed capture through as text.** The parameter's declared type would then be
  false: a `Slug $slug` capture would arrive as a `tainted string`, and every handler would repeat the
  conversion the declaration already names.
- **A `null` capture for a segment the class refuses.** It needs `tryParse` at the binding site and
  hands every handler a nullable it did not declare, moving the failure to wherever the program first
  dereferences it.
- **A regex constraint on a capture**, now or later. An application-authored pattern over the
  request path runs before any rate limiting, which makes catastrophic backtracking an
  unauthenticated denial of service; a closed set is spelled as a set of allowed values or a subset
  of an enum's cases instead ([`routing/a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set`](routing.md#routing-a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set)).

<sub>See also [`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation), [`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](security.md#security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning), [`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types).</sub>

<a id="security-derived-codec-qualifiers"></a>

## A derived codec adds no qualifier rule, a JSON decoder fills a `secret` property, and a call that encodes one does not compile

`rule:security/derived-codec-qualifiers`

A derived codec introduces no qualifier rule of its own. A decoder assigns into declared property
types, so a payload that carries `tainted` requires the fields receiving it to declare it, and the
check happens where the qualifier is statically known — the **call site** that decodes, not inside the
codec. Only `string` and `bytes` carry a qualifier, so an integer, a decimal, an enum or an instant
field needs nothing. Declaring `tainted` on a decoded field is friction at the moment somebody is
trying to be quick, and it is the same declaration hand-written hydration already needed; the derive
is only where a newcomer meets it first.

A member that reads its own payload decides by its owner: every `Core\Request` decoder,
`Core\Http\Response::jsonAs`, `Core\Jwt::verifyIssued`, and `queryAs` and `streamAs` on a
`Core\Db\Connection` or `Core\Db\Transaction` carry `tainted` always. A row's text is input because
an earlier request may have stored it ([`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources)), so a `#[Db\Derive]` class or
an inline shape fills a text column only into a `tainted` field. A field no column maps is refused
by its type instead, and gets no second report. `Core\Arr::shapeAs`
converts the array it is handed, so its argument decides: by the test an encoder applies
([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)), an array whose type carries `tainted` or `mixed` anywhere, or a
literal holding such a value, requires every text field it fills to be `tainted` (`E0810`). An
`array<string>` or a literal of the program's own values fills a plain `string`. A literal element that
is a call is read as outside text, because its type is not kept there; binding it to a typed variable
first is the fix. `Core\Json::decodeAs` decides by its document the same way: a `tainted string`
document is admitted, and every text field it fills must be `tainted` (`E0810`), while the program's
own `string` fills a plain field. Admitting the document launders nothing, because the class it
answers carries the mark in each field that receives text.

A `secret` property on a `#[Json\Derive]` class is a field its decoder fills, so a login form read
through `jsonAs` or `postAs` lands its password in a `secret tainted string` and the debug record
replaces it ([`testing/a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced`](testing.md#testing-a-recorded-request-keeps-its-input-with-credentials-replaced)). Encoding
was already a sink ([`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse)), and it stays one: a call of
`Core\Json::encode` or `Core\Response::json` whose argument's type reaches such a class, through an
array, a shape, a union or another field, is `E0462` at the call, naming the property. A value the
checker cannot see through, one typed `mixed` or handed to an encoder in a bag, is refused by the
encoder when it reaches the object, by the class's `secret` bits, with a `LogicError` naming the
property. A class that writes its own encoder decides for itself, and skipping the property keeps the
class encodable. So such a class has a decoder and no usable derived encoder.

A `#[Db\Derive]` class keeps the refusal at the declaration: a row is read and written by the same
derive, so a `secret` property there is `E0462` where it is written, with skipping it as the fix.

Trade-offs: one walk of the argument's type per encode call at compile time, and at run time one scan
of a class's slot bits per object encoded whose class has a `secret` property.

**Declined:** keeping the declaration refusal for JSON. It made the replacement in a recorded body
unreachable, because no derived decoder could fill a `secret` property, so a password decoded with
`jsonAs` sat in a plain `tainted string`.

<sub>See also [`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse), [`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation), [`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources).</sub>

<a id="security-assert-trusted"></a>

## `Core\Taint::assertTrusted` is the one generic way out, and it carries a written reason at the call site

`rule:security/assert-trusted`

`Core\Taint::assertTrusted(tainted string, string $reason): string` is the one generic escape from the
qualifier, for the case where the developer has validated the value themselves and needs to say so. It
is modelled on this project's own `unsafe` policy: forbidden by default, rare, greppable, and carrying
a written reason at the call site rather than a silent cast. Its `bytes` form is a second member,
`Core\Taint::assertTrustedBytes(tainted bytes, string $reason): bytes`, under the same rules, as
`Core\Secret::revealBytes` is `reveal`'s; its case is a program decoding with `Core\Serialize::decode`
the bytes it encoded itself ([`classes/serialize-is-a-closed-format`](classes.md#classes-serialize-is-a-closed-format)).

It is the answer at every position that has no launderer *and cannot have one* — a metric label, whose
hazard is unbounded cardinality rather than content ([`security/metric-label-refuses-tainted`](security.md#security-metric-label-refuses-tainted)); a
regex pattern, where no transform makes an attacker-authored pattern safe
([`security/regex-pattern-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-regex-pattern-is-a-sink)); a format template drawn from a translation catalogue
([`security/every-grammar-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-every-grammar-is-a-sink)).

It removes `tainted` and nothing else: a `secret` operand is refused there, because confidentiality is
a separate axis and this member makes no claim about it.

<sub>See also [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`security/every-grammar-is-a-sink`](security.md#security-every-grammar-is-a-sink), [`security/metric-label-refuses-tainted`](security.md#security-metric-label-refuses-tainted).</sub>

<a id="security-response-body-is-one-typed-member"></a>

## A response body is written by one typed member, and mixing `echo` with one of them does not compile

`rule:security/response-body-is-one-typed-member`

A response body is written by one of seven typed members, each owning a body shape and setting its own
content type. The HTML member takes the carrier and so has nothing to refuse; the JSON and text
members are contagious; the bytes member is contagious in its body and a sink in its content type; the
file member's path is a sink.

**Two of the seven write their body over time rather than at once, and classification follows the
shape and not the timing.** The streaming member declares a media type it is told, so that argument
is the bytes member's sink for the bytes member's reason — it becomes an instruction the peer obeys
about how to read everything after it — while each chunk, text or bytes, is a sink and refuses a
tainted argument. The text member may accept a tainted body because its media type is fixed at
`text/plain`; a stream's media type is whatever the program declared, `text/html` included, so a
chunk is markup the peer may parse. The text member accepts a tainted body and a chunk does not.

The event-stream member takes no media type — the protocol's is the only one it could have — and its
`send` splits three ways. The payload is contagious, for the JSON member's reason: framing belongs to
us and to the serializer, and normalization happens before the payload is split across `data:` lines,
so it cannot reach any other line. The event name and the id are **sinks**: a client dispatches on
the name and echoes the id back in its next request's `Last-Event-ID`, so an attacker-chosen one is
the cross-tenant hazard a tainted topic name is.

**Every way a call could corrupt an event's framing throws a `LogicError`, and none is repaired.** An
event name or id carrying `\n`, `\r` or NUL is refused: stripping the byte would change the name a
client dispatches on, and a client discards an id containing a NUL outright. An empty payload is
refused, because a client does not dispatch an event whose data buffer is empty, so the send could
never arrive. A status set on a path that opens an event stream is refused, because an event stream
is `200` by protocol. The streaming member takes any status, so that refusal is the event stream's
alone.

The JSON member accepts a tainted value freely, because the framing belongs to the serializer and
never to concatenation — a tainted string becomes a JSON string value and cannot escape it. The text
member accepts one only because a no-sniff header is on by default with nothing configured, so
`text/plain` is not re-parsed as HTML; that dependency is stated so removing the default is visibly a
change to two rules.

**Two writers of one response body is a compile error** — `echo` beside a typed member, and two
different typed members beside each other. A file's text outside `<?nvs … ?>` is `echo`'s writer
here, because the HTML sink writes it the same way. They disagree about the body's type and its content type,
and silently letting the last one win is how a JSON endpoint acquires an HTML prelude. What the
refusal needs is two *different* writers: one member called twice declares one thing twice, so a body
written in a loop is an ordinary program and is left alone.

**That error is reported where a response is statically certain, which is a `#[Route]` handler.**
`echo` is bound by context and not by syntax — the same body writes a response under a request and a
terminal sink under `nvs run` — so a method that is not a handler writes no response for two writers
to disagree over and is left alone rather than refused on suspicion. One response is outside the
check and stays there: a mount's entry script, whose top-level frame is the request body and which is
the same compiled unit the command line runs, so nothing distinguishes the two uses at compile time.
There the default decides instead of the refusal — `echo` alone means `text/html`, and a typed member
written beside it wins the content type it declared last.

**The file member, `sendFile(string $path)`, takes the path alone.** A download name is a
`Content-Disposition` header, which `setHeader` already admits, and what the file's bytes are called
is the static-file policy's media-type table, which also owns its `Range` and conditional handling.

- **Memory:** a file body costs the request one path, and the connection one open handle and one
  range's read buffer while the response is in flight. The file is never copied through the request.

**Declined:**
- **A filename parameter on the file member.** A download name is a header, and `setHeader` writes it.
- **A content-type parameter on the file member.** It would let a response declare one type while
  the static-file policy's range and conditional handling served the same path as another.
- **Keying the body's rule on its `Content-Type` rather than on the member that wrote it.** The header
  can be set after the first byte of the body is written, so the rule would depend on a fact not yet
  decided where it must be enforced.
- **One `Response::write` that takes `Core\Html\Markup` for every body.** One rule instead of several
  members, but it makes [`security/assert-trusted`](security.md#security-assert-trusted) the ordinary way to write an API handler, which
