- **Memory:** a `Jwt\KeySet` holds at most 16 public keys for as long as the program holds it, and a
  verification costs at most one signature check. Nothing is held between calls.

**Declined:**
- **Trying every key in a `Jwt\KeySet`.** It would let a token with no `kid` verify against a large set,
  and it makes verification cost linear in a number the token's sender influences. A single-key set for
  a token with no `kid` gives the same guarantee without the loop.
- **The JWS JSON serialization, and a detached or unencoded payload.** `b64` is refused in a header for
  that reason, and compact serialization is the one form read.
- **JWE-encrypted ID tokens.** They are rare and opt-in at every provider, and they need RSA-OAEP
  ([`core-classes/crypto-interop-tier`](core-classes.md#core-classes-crypto-interop-tier)).

<sub>See also [`security/algorithm-comes-from-the-key`](security.md#security-algorithm-comes-from-the-key), [`security/jwt-expiry-is-mandatory`](security.md#security-jwt-expiry-is-mandatory), [`security/verification-does-not-launder`](security.md#security-verification-does-not-launder), [`security/derived-codec-qualifiers`](security.md#security-derived-codec-qualifiers), [`security/jwe-compact-subset`](security.md#security-jwe-compact-subset).</sub>

<a id="security-csrf-is-on-by-default"></a>

## The server refuses an unsafe verb without a valid CSRF token, and the opt-out is written on the route itself

`rule:security/csrf-is-on-by-default`

The server refuses an unsafe verb — the four that change state — without a valid token, using the
match it already made to know which handler is which. Generation and constant-time verification belong
to the protocol roster ([`security/protocol-roster`](security.md#security-protocol-roster)); this decides only the default, and the
default is on with nothing configured.

**The refusal has two grounds, and what arms each of them differs.** A covered request whose `Origin`
names somewhere other than where it arrived is refused with nothing configured at all — that is the
forgery this is named for, and it reads only headers the request brought. A covered request without a
token this deployment issued, bound to the session it rides under, is refused as soon as `[http]
csrf_key` names the key that says what a valid token is; until it does, there is no expected token for
any request to be missing. A valid token passes whatever the origin says, because it proves the page
the request came from was this application's.

**The origin half covers every unsafe verb, matched or not.** A program with no `#[Route]` table,
and a path a routed program's table does not claim, get the same origin refusal a matched row gets.
The origin is judged before `Core\Router::dispatch` asks whether a route matched, so a cross-origin
unsafe write to an unclaimed path is `Refusal::Csrf`, never `NotFound`, and `NotFound` is a
same-origin request, one with no `Origin`, or a safe verb.
The token half applies only to a matched row, because the opt-out is written on a route: a program
with no table could not exempt a webhook from it, and every write it serves under a key would be
refused.

**The session a token is bound to is read the way `Core\Session::start` reads it**: the cookie
`[session] cookie` names, found on any `Cookie` line, pair by pair, with one reader for both. Two
readers that split the header differently would check a token against one session while the program
opens another. **A request with no session passes no token**, from any origin. A token for no session
is what a page shows a visitor who has none, so anyone can load one, and accepting it would let
another site sign a visitor in to an account the attacker chose.

**A page issues a token with `Core\Csrf::token`**, after `Core\Session::start`. It binds the token to
the identifier the response's session cookie carries, under `[http] csrf_key` read by the door's own
reader, so the token it renders is one the door accepts on the next request. For a visitor with no
session, the call is the session's first write: it draws the identifier and sends the cookie, so a
login form shown to a new visitor is bound to an identifier too. `token` before `start` throws naming
`start`, and with no key it throws naming `[http] csrf_key`. `Core\Csrf::issue` stays for a program
that binds a token to a value of its own and checks it itself with `verify`.

**The token rides in the `x-csrf-token` header, a `_csrf` query parameter or an urlencoded form's
`_csrf` field**, and the first of the three present decides. A plain HTML form therefore needs no
script. The form body is read only for a checked `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` request that
sent neither of the other two, up to `[limits] request_body`, by the request's own task before the
handler runs, and the handler reads the same form afterwards. A body past the limit is refused as a
missing token. A multipart body is never read for a token: a file upload would have to be buffered
whole before the check, on the sender's terms, so a multipart write carries its token in the header or
the query. **What it spends:** up to `[limits] request_body` per such request in flight, attributed to
that request, and bytes the handler's own form parse would have buffered anyway.

**An upgrade is checked by its origin, on any verb.** A browser opens a WebSocket with a `GET` that
carries the visitor's cookies, so a request asking to upgrade that matched a route is refused when its
`Origin` names somewhere other than where it arrived, and passes with no `Origin`, as a write does. The
token half does not apply to it, key or no key, because a browser's handshake cannot carry the token
header; the write check a verb owes still follows, so an upgrade header takes nothing off it.

What a deployment that names no key therefore does **not** refuse is a covered request that sent no
`Origin` — every non-browser client, and so every API caller. Naming the key is what covers it. A key
written so the door cannot read it is refused at boot rather than left unarmed, because a deployment
whose configuration says the check is on and whose door verifies nothing is the one way this must not
fail.

A route that legitimately needs no token — a webhook authenticated by signature, an API authenticated
by a bearer token — says so **in its own declaration**, per route, in the attribute that route already
carries: never a group and never a configuration key. The same `csrf: false` turns off the upgrade
check, for a socket other sites are meant to open. Writing it on the route is what keeps the
exemption reviewable next to the handler it exempts.

**The refusal is the door's, and a program may only answer it.** In a program that calls
`Core\Router::dispatch`, the refused request still runs the entry, in refusal mode: `route()` answers
`null`, there is no body, and `dispatch` calls the gate's `refused` with `Refusal::Csrf` after setting
`403` ([`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler)). The gate chooses the page, the status and a
log line, so a form sent after its session expired can show the user what happened. No handler runs,
and a gate that throws leaves the empty `403`. A program that does not call `dispatch` gets the empty
`403`, because it would read the refused request as an ordinary one with no route.

**Declined:**
- **Enforcing only when a session cookie is present.** It sounds tighter, since forgery can only
  target cookie-authenticated requests, but it makes protection depend on what the client sent rather
  than on what the code says, which is harder to reason about and harder to test.
- **Tokens available, and enforcement left to the program.** An unprotected state-changing route would
  look the same as a protected one at compile time and at run time.
- **Reading a multipart body for its `_csrf` field.** Every upload would be buffered before the check,
  up to `[limits] upload_total`, before anything decides whether to run it.
- **A gate that lets a refused request through.** The exemption would then live in code a reviewer reads
  apart from the route. `csrf: false` on the route stays the only opt-out.

<sub>See also [`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](security.md#security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning), [`security/protocol-roster`](security.md#security-protocol-roster), [`attributes/access-payload`](attributes.md#attributes-access-payload), [`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler).</sub>

<a id="security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning"></a>

## The compiler proves a route's access decision was written, never that it was honoured

`rule:security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`

The compiler verifies that a route's access attribute is there and that the name inside it resolves.
It never asks what the name means, never calls anything, and has no opinion about roles, policies or
sessions. An omission is an error rather than a public default — that half is
[`attributes/access-is-a-required-sibling`](attributes.md#attributes-access-is-a-required-sibling), and the payload's shape is
[`attributes/access-payload`](attributes.md#attributes-access-payload).

**Interpretation belongs to whoever dispatches.** The declared name rides on the match the server made
as uninterpreted data, and the application reads and enforces it once, in front of every handler, so
a route whose handler never mentions access is still checked. Under `Core\Router::dispatch` that place
is the gate's `allows`, which runs before every handler the generated jump calls
([`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler)); a hand-written dispatcher checks it above its
`switch`.
**A dispatcher compares a case, never text:** `Core\Router\Match::accessAs<E>()` answers the decision
as a case of the enum `E` and `null` for any other decision, so a renamed case is a compile error at
the comparison and an admin route never reads as a public one. A case reaching `mixed` is only its
integer ([`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation)), which is why the typed member names its enum rather than
answering `mixed`. `access()` answers the resolved name as a `string`, for a log line and for a class
constant, which has no enum. A type argument that is not an enum is **`E0841`**. An application that
mixes `Core\Audience::Public` with its own roles asks once per enum, and reads `null` as denied. A
comparison against the text keeps compiling after the case it names is renamed, never matches again,
and serves the route unguarded, so text is the reading for a log line only. **The server enforces
CSRF and nothing else** ([`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default)): interpreting a role would need a
session, a user model and a role source, all three of which are deliberately outside the binary. Two
enforcement points is how a route ends up checked twice in development and not at all in production,
so there is one.

**The limit is stated rather than implied: the compiler guarantees the decision was *written*, not
that it was *honoured*.** `Core\Router::dispatch` is the dispatch site that closes this for a program
that calls it: no handler runs unless `allows` returned `true` for its match, so a gate that reads the
access decision enforces it on every route. What `allows` concludes stays the application's. An
application that hand-rolls dispatch and never reads the access name gets no enforcement from anyone,
because the compiler cannot follow a dispatch table a program builds from data.

Object-level authorisation is outside it too. Most privilege escalation is a request for a row that
belongs to another user, and no language-level mechanism answers that, because the check needs the
row. The handler that loads the row makes that check.

- **Memory:** `accessAs<E>()` allocates nothing per call: the enum's name is an immortal string
  constant of the unit. The work is one comparison of the row's enum name against the written one and,
  when they are equal, a linear search of the unit's enums by name.

**Declined:**
- **`access(): mixed` answering the constant's value.** A case in `mixed` is its backing integer, so
  `Core\Audience::Public` and `App\Role::Admin` are both `0` there, and a `match` would take the
  public arm for the admin route.
- **`access(Class::class): ?E`, typed from a string argument.** The checker would type a result from
  an argument's value, a special case no other member has, for the answer a written type argument
  already gives.
- **Keeping the text and teaching the comparison.** The silent rename stays, and that is the bug.
- **The decision readable only through `Core\Attributes::get` on the handler.** That call names the
  method, so the check is written once per `switch` arm. An arm that forgets it is an unguarded route,
  and nothing reports the omission.
- **A compile error where an access decision is never read.** The compiler recognises `dispatch`, but
  it cannot follow a dispatch table a program builds from data, and a gate's `allows` may decide on
  something other than the access name.

<sub>See also [`attributes/access-is-a-required-sibling`](attributes.md#attributes-access-is-a-required-sibling), [`attributes/access-payload`](attributes.md#attributes-access-payload), [`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default), [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type), [`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler).</sub>

<a id="security-bidi-predicate"></a>

## A span is rejected when it ends with a directional scope still open, decided by two counters

`rule:security/bidi-predicate`

Nine code points open or close a directional scope: four embedding and override forms closed by one
terminator, and three isolate forms closed by another. Two more are marks rather than scopes and are
**not** covered, because they open nothing and therefore cannot be unterminated.

| Code points | Role | Closed by |
|---|---|---|
| U+202A `LRE`, U+202B `RLE`, U+202D `LRO`, U+202E `RLO` | embedding and override, the legacy forms every published exploit uses | U+202C `PDF` |
| U+2066 `LRI`, U+2067 `RLI`, U+2068 `FSI` | isolate, the forms Unicode recommends | U+2069 `PDI` |
| U+200E `LRM`, U+200F `RLM` | mark: changes one character's resolved direction and opens no scope | *not covered* |

**A span is rejected when it ends with a scope still open.** Two independent counters, one for
embeddings and overrides and one for isolates: an opener increments, the matching terminator
decrements with a floor of zero, and both must be zero at the end of the span. A stray terminator
with no opener closes nothing and opens nothing, so it is accepted.

The attack is Trojan Source: text that renders in an order its bytes do not have, so a reviewer
approves one program and the compiler builds another. Code review is the control being defeated, and
the published exploits live in comments and string literals. Identifiers are ASCII-only, which
closes homoglyph and bidi identifiers structurally; what is left is comments, string literals,
inline-HTML text and runtime data, and the condition is the same in all four. The line is drawn at
*unterminated*, not at *present*, the line other compilers draw too, because balanced controls are
what legitimate Arabic, Hebrew and mixed-direction text uses.

This is deliberately simpler than the full bidirectional algorithm, whose directional status stack has
interactions the counters flatten. That is correct here because the question is not *how does this
render* — which needs the real algorithm — but *does this span leave a scope open*, which the counters
answer soundly. The simplification can only over-approximate towards rejecting, which is the safe
direction. It costs nothing measurable: two counters carried through a walk that happens anyway, no
allocation and no table lookup.

**Declined:**
- **Rejecting the eleven code points outright, terminated or not.** It breaks legitimate
  mixed-direction literals: an Arabic message interpolating a Latin name needs an isolate to render
  correctly. It also pushes developers to build such strings by concatenation to get past the check.
- **The full bidirectional algorithm.** The question is whether a scope is left open, not how the
  span renders ([`security/bidi-scope-is-the-whole-target`](security.md#security-bidi-scope-is-the-whole-target)).

<sub>See also [`security/bidi-boundaries`](security.md#security-bidi-boundaries), [`security/bidi-scope-is-the-whole-target`](security.md#security-bidi-scope-is-the-whole-target), [`errors/record-transformations`](errors.md#errors-record-transformations).</sub>

<a id="security-bidi-boundaries"></a>

## The lexer refuses an unterminated control and the sinks substitute it, and nobody writes a second predicate

`rule:security/bidi-boundaries`

The predicate has one implementation and several callers. **The lexer is an error**: one token — a
string literal, a comment, or an inline-HTML run — and additionally each line inside a multi-line one,
so a heredoc cannot hide a scope across its lines. A doc comment is that same span and reuses that
same check rather than growing a second one, so the tools that render one emit text the lexer has
already accepted. **The sinks substitute**: terminal output, whose span is one `echo` operand or one
`Core\Cli::write` call, and `Core\Html::escape`, whose span is one call, each replace an unmatched
control with `�` (U+FFFD). The diagnostic record applies the same predicate once, when a record is
built, so a log line, a dump and a stack trace carry the same answer into every rendering
([`errors/record-transformations`](errors.md#errors-record-transformations)). Deciding the rule separately at each caller is how one rule
acquires several slightly different definitions, so a second copy of the predicate is a bug.

The asymmetry is deliberate. Source is written by a developer who can fix it, and a failed build names
the file and line; runtime data arrives from outside, where refusing to print it would turn a display
concern into an availability one. Substituting rather than deleting keeps the property that a
neutralized byte is *visible* — the reader sees that something was removed instead of silently reading
a shorter string.

**No suppression at the lexer.** A file that legitimately needs an unterminated control does not
exist, and an attribute that switched off a security check would be the first exception this project
grants.

**Declined:**
- **A warning rather than an error at the lexer.** A warning nobody fails a build on is not a
  control, and the project has no suppression story for spelling rules
  ([`core-api/identifier-casing`](core-api.md#core-api-identifier-casing)).
- **Handling it only in `nvs fmt`.** The formatter is never wired into `nvs check`
  ([`tooling/fmt-is-one-canonical-style`](tooling.md#tooling-fmt-is-one-canonical-style)), so a formatter-only rule is one an attacker's change
  simply does not run.
- **Handling it only at the sinks, not in source.** That inverts the severity: the source case is the
  one with a working exploit against code review, and the runtime cases are display deception.

<sub>See also [`security/bidi-predicate`](security.md#security-bidi-predicate), [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`errors/record-transformations`](errors.md#errors-record-transformations).</sub>

<a id="security-bidi-scope-is-the-whole-target"></a>

## Zero-width characters, homoglyphs and the full bidirectional algorithm are deliberately outside the check

`rule:security/bidi-scope-is-the-whole-target`

Three neighbouring hazards are deliberately outside the check, and saying so is what stops a future
session from adding a fourth mechanism.

**Zero-width and invisible characters** (U+200B `ZWSP`, U+200C `ZWNJ`, U+200D `ZWJ`, U+2060 `WJ`,
U+FEFF) are not targeted: the false-positive cost is real — one is
*required* in Persian, another in Indic scripts and in every multi-codepoint emoji sequence — and with
identifiers ASCII-only they can no longer make two names look alike. They can pad a string, which is a
deception with no mechanism behind it. **Homoglyphs** are closed structurally by the ASCII identifier
rule, so a confusables table would be dead weight. **The full bidirectional algorithm** is not
implemented, because Novis does not render text.

With the predicate's callers in place, the language is closed against the Trojan Source class —
identifiers by construction, everything else by the predicate. One cost is accepted and named: an
editor or diff viewer that does not itself neutralize these controls still misrenders a file *before*
the compiler sees it, so the check protects the merge and not the reading.

<sub>See also [`security/bidi-predicate`](security.md#security-bidi-predicate), [`security/bidi-boundaries`](security.md#security-bidi-boundaries).</sub>

<a id="security-hash-writes-argon2id-only"></a>

## `hash` writes Argon2id and nothing else, and no member takes an algorithm argument

`rule:security/hash-writes-argon2id-only`

Hashing writes one algorithm and nothing else, and **no member gains an algorithm argument**. Novis
never *produces* a legacy hash; it only stops refusing to read one
([`security/bcrypt-read-roster`](security.md#security-bcrypt-read-roster)).

An algorithm parameter is how a deployment ends up writing the weaker of two options for the lifetime
of the code that passed it, and it is a parameter no caller is in a position to choose well. Removing
it means the write side has one behaviour to reason about and the read side carries the whole
compatibility surface — which is the only place compatibility belongs, because a stored row was
written by somebody else.

The write-side parameters and their reasons live with the implementation rather than being spelled at
a call site, so raising them is one change rather than a sweep.

**Declined:**
- **An algorithm argument, or a bcrypt write path.** Either reopens the copied-call-site problem the
  class exists to close, and no new hash should ever be bcrypt.

<sub>See also [`security/bcrypt-read-roster`](security.md#security-bcrypt-read-roster), [`security/needs-rehash-answers-weaker`](security.md#security-needs-rehash-answers-weaker).</sub>

<a id="security-bcrypt-read-roster"></a>

## A stored password hash is read from a roster of exactly two shapes, and the roster grows only by amendment

`rule:security/bcrypt-read-roster`

Verification accepts exactly two stored shapes: the modern hash this library writes, and a bcrypt hash
under the `$2y$`, `$2a$` or `$2b$` prefix — one algorithm under three tags, verified identically. **The
roster grows only by amending this rule, never by accepting what a parser happens to read.**

`$2x$` is refused: it exists to be bug-compatible with `crypt_blowfish`'s sign-extension overflow, and
verifying it means reimplementing the bug.

bcrypt is on the roster because it is what a real population's column holds. PHP's `PASSWORD_DEFAULT`
has written bcrypt since `password_hash` appeared, and Argon2 never became the default, so the user
table of almost every migrating application is a bcrypt column. Without a read path that population
would catch the unreadable-hash throw around every verification, which launders the storage-bug signal
the throw exists to raise ([`security/an-unreadable-stored-hash-throws`](security.md#security-an-unreadable-stored-hash-throws)), or build a dual-column
scheme by hand.

This is what lets an existing user table, hashed by another runtime, verify on day one and rewrite itself one
successful login at a time ([`security/needs-rehash-answers-weaker`](security.md#security-needs-rehash-answers-weaker)). The reader is a pure-Rust
bcrypt crate with a constant-time comparison of the digest.

- **Memory:** about 4 KiB, the eksblowfish key schedule, held transiently per verification of a legacy
  row on the calling task. It is bounded by in-flight logins, and shrinks as the table converges.

**Declined:**
- **Reading every algorithm a verifier library can read.** Each entry is a parser, an attack surface and
  a promise kept forever, and two shapes cover the migrating population. A third shape is added the way
  bcrypt was: by being what a real population's column holds.
- **An offline tool that converts the column.** A stored hash is not invertible, so only a presented
  password can be rehashed, and the login-time loop is the only migration path.
- **A bcrypt write path.** No new hash should ever be bcrypt ([`security/hash-writes-argon2id-only`](security.md#security-hash-writes-argon2id-only)).

<sub>See also [`security/hash-writes-argon2id-only`](security.md#security-hash-writes-argon2id-only), [`security/needs-rehash-answers-weaker`](security.md#security-needs-rehash-answers-weaker), [`security/an-unreadable-stored-hash-throws`](security.md#security-an-unreadable-stored-hash-throws).</sub>

<a id="security-needs-rehash-answers-weaker"></a>

## `needsRehash` measures weaker rather than different, so every bcrypt hash asks to be rewritten

`rule:security/needs-rehash-answers-weaker`

`needsRehash` answers whether the stored hash is **weaker** than what hashing writes now, not whether
its parameters differ. A different algorithm is weaker by that rule's own terms, so a legacy hash
always answers `true`.

With the read roster that completes a migration with no flag, no tool and no second code path:
verification proves the password, this member says the row has fallen behind, hashing rewrites it, and
the legacy column converges to empty. A stored hash is not invertible, so a presented password at
login is the only point where a row can be rewritten, and this loop is the migration. It reads a legacy hash rather than throwing at it, which is the
one behaviour this member owes the roster.

A check that compares the stored parameters for difference answers `true` when a deployment
*lowers* its cost as readily as when it raises it. Measuring weakness rather than difference is the
direction that never rewrites a strong row into a weaker one.

<sub>See also [`security/bcrypt-read-roster`](security.md#security-bcrypt-read-roster), [`security/hash-writes-argon2id-only`](security.md#security-hash-writes-argon2id-only).</sub>

<a id="security-bcrypt-cost-ceiling"></a>

## A stored bcrypt cost above 17 is refused before any work is done

`rule:security/bcrypt-cost-ceiling`

A stored bcrypt hash carries its own cost, and the cost is the base-2 logarithm of the round count — a
CPU-time lever one `UPDATE` away from anyone who can write the table. Verification refuses a stored
cost above **17** before doing any work, as an ordinary throw.

Seventeen is far above the 10 to 13 real deployments write and far below the minutes of CPU per
verification that the format's maximum of 31 costs, so it costs no real table anything and closes the denial of service. Refusing *before*
any work is what makes it a defence rather than a report: a check made afterwards has already spent
the CPU the attacker was buying.

The same shape guards the modern algorithm's memory parameter, which is the reason this is a ceiling
on a stored value rather than a validation of a written one.

<sub>See also [`security/bcrypt-read-roster`](security.md#security-bcrypt-read-roster), [`security/an-unreadable-stored-hash-throws`](security.md#security-an-unreadable-stored-hash-throws), [`errors/escalation-ladder`](errors.md#errors-escalation-ladder).</sub>

<a id="security-bcrypt-truncation"></a>

## bcrypt's 72-byte truncation is replicated exactly, because the stored row was written under it

`rule:security/bcrypt-truncation`

bcrypt hashes at most 72 bytes of a password and stops at a NUL byte. Verification replicates that
exactly, because it must accept precisely the passwords the other implementation accepted against the
same stored row — it is the algorithm's behaviour, not a choice being made here.

Replicating it is the correct answer and an uncomfortable one, which is why it is written down: a
password longer than the limit has a suffix that never mattered, and two passwords sharing their first
72 bytes both verify. That is one more reason every such row is marked for rehash under an algorithm
without the edge ([`security/needs-rehash-answers-weaker`](security.md#security-needs-rehash-answers-weaker)).

<sub>See also [`security/bcrypt-read-roster`](security.md#security-bcrypt-read-roster), [`security/needs-rehash-answers-weaker`](security.md#security-needs-rehash-answers-weaker).</sub>

<a id="security-an-unreadable-stored-hash-throws"></a>

## A stored value outside the read roster throws, and the message never quotes the bytes

`rule:security/an-unreadable-stored-hash-throws`

A stored value outside the read roster — garbage, a refused prefix, or a hash naming any other
algorithm — **throws** rather than answering `false`, and the message never quotes the bytes
([`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse)).

The two outcomes are different facts. "This password is wrong" is an answer about a credential; "this
column does not hold a hash I can read" is a fact about the deployment, and collapsing them into
`false` means every user of a mis-migrated table simply fails to log in, silently, until somebody
notices. A throw wakes an operator ([`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused)).

The roster having two entries instead of one does not change that property; it moves where the
boundary sits, and this rule is the boundary's home.

**Declined:**
- **Answering `false` for an unreadable stored value, as PHP does.** It hides the storage bug behind
  the login screen, and widening the roster gives no reason to reopen that.

<sub>See also [`security/bcrypt-read-roster`](security.md#security-bcrypt-read-roster), [`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse), [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused).</sub>

<a id="security-a-session-id-the-store-did-not-issue-is-rejected"></a>

## A session id the store did not issue is rejected, always, with no toggle

`rule:security/a-session-id-the-store-did-not-issue-is-rejected`

`Core\Session::start()` accepts a presented id only if its own store issued it and it is still
live. An unknown, expired or attacker-minted id is discarded and a fresh, empty session is opened in
its place. Its new id is drawn when something is first written to it
([`core-classes/session-is-started-explicitly`](core-classes.md#core-classes-session-is-started-explicitly)), so the presented id is never used.
There is no toggle, no ini, no option, on the security priority: an off switch for fixation
resistance is a security default traded for nothing. Session fixation resistance is therefore a
property of the language, not of a deployment's configuration.

It follows that the session store must be able to answer "did I issue this id". A store that holds
nothing, such as a signed cookie carrying the record itself, cannot answer it and so cannot be the
session store ([`core-api/session-roster`](core-api.md#core-api-session-roster)). `nvs_stdlib::session`'s test
`start_opens_a_held_record_and_a_fresh_one_for_an_id_the_store_does_not_hold` presents a forged id
and gets a fresh session that does not carry it.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/session-is-started-explicitly`](core-classes.md#core-classes-session-is-started-explicitly), [`core-api/session-roster`](core-api.md#core-api-session-roster).</sub>
